items.text: The school is conceived as two distinct daily environments joined by a shared assembly crossing. One is a vertical academic house for ordinary teaching; the other is a smaller care and cultural house for focused support, making, and reading. The commons between them is a destination in its own right, with a defined passage across its perimeter linking the two houses. The classroom house rises three storeys; the care house rises two, with administration and arts at grade and reading above. Between them, gym and dining remain ground-based double-height volumes. Core academic and special education occupy separate end houses rather than sharing teaching floors. Administration accompanies special education, while the commons is the sole built mediator between both houses.

The school is conceived as two distinct daily environments joined by a shared assembly crossing. One is a vertical academic house for ordinary teaching; the other is a smaller care and cultural house for focused support, making, and reading. The commons between them is a destination in its own right, with a defined passage across its perimeter linking the two houses. The scheme seeks to make communal activity a deliberate transition between different learning environments while allowing specialized support to retain an identifiable and quieter home.

A raised cultural house acts as an inhabited bridge between a teaching house and a communal base. Unlike a compact triangular cluster, the school is organized as two separated destinations connected by a third elevated cultural layer. The bridge provides a distinct shared destination while the hall remains an independent double-height volume below its own roof, not the supporting base for an arts loft. The teaching house rises three floors with classrooms throughout. The cultural connector rises from an administrative ground floor through arts to reading at its crown. The communal house remains double height at grade. Core academic and special education occupy the teaching house. Administration anchors the connecting cultural house, while the gym and dining share the separate commons house at the opposite end of the connection.

A raised cultural house acts as an inhabited bridge between a teaching house and a communal base. Unlike a compact triangular cluster, the school is organized as two separated destinations connected by a third elevated cultural layer. The bridge provides a distinct shared destination while the hall remains an independent double-height volume below its own roof, not the supporting base for an arts loft. Seeks to make creative and reading activities a visible connection between learning and assembly, encouraging shared cultural use while distinguishing public gatherings from the quieter daily teaching environment.

A dedicated cultural threshold stands between two sharply different destinations: a consolidated academic house and a communal assembly hall. Unlike a conventional civic gateway, the threshold is primarily a place of making, student care and reading, while the school's administrative front remains embedded within the academic house. This separates the symbolic cultural entrance from the operational point of school oversight. The academic house rises three floors, with administration and teaching at grade and more classrooms above. The cultural threshold rises to an upper library over ground-floor arts, while the commons remains double-height. Core academic, special education and administration share the learning house. A cultural threshold separates them from the gym and dining, positioning creative learning and student care between everyday teaching and collective assembly.

A dedicated cultural threshold stands between two sharply different destinations: a consolidated academic house and a communal assembly hall. Unlike a conventional civic gateway, the threshold is primarily a place of making, student care and reading, while the school's administrative front remains embedded within the academic house. This separates the symbolic cultural entrance from the operational point of school oversight. The scheme seeks to give creative learning a recognizable shared address while allowing administration to remain closely tied to classrooms and placing community assembly beyond a cultural transition.

Two distinct teaching houses stand alongside a third, shared civic spine. Rather than treating specialized learning as an appendage of general classrooms, the houses are peers, each directly connected to the spine but not to one another. The spine combines the school's public threshold and collective gathering spaces, making a common institutional address for two different learning environments. Both teaching houses rise three floors, with their learning spaces beginning at grade. The civic spine holds administration and the double-height commons at grade, with the media center forming an upper reading level. Core academic and special education occupy separate teaching houses connected through the civic spine. Administration shares that spine with the gym and dining, placing common oversight between the two learning populations.

Two distinct teaching houses stand alongside a third, shared civic spine. Rather than treating specialized learning as an appendage of general classrooms, the houses are peers, each directly connected to the spine but not to one another. The spine combines the school's public threshold and collective gathering spaces, making a common institutional address for two different learning environments. The scheme seeks to establish equivalent identities for general and specialized learning while concentrating shared services and community activities at a common, supervised point of access.

The school is conceived as a paired everyday teaching and assembly building alongside a separate, vertically organized inclusion house. The attached pair establishes the collective school routine, while the independent house offers another scale of occupation for focused support and small-group learning. Their relationship is that of neighboring institutions on shared grounds, not an enclosed three-part circulation network. All three masses reach three storeys. Classrooms rise through the learning mass; the commons carries double-height gathering spaces below an upper reading level. The separate support house stacks special education above its ground-level care facilities. Core academic occupies a three-level teaching mass directly connected to gym and dining, which also share the administrative front. Special education sits in a separate house, with no enclosed connection to either.

The school is conceived as a paired everyday teaching and assembly building alongside a separate, vertically organized inclusion house. The attached pair establishes the collective school routine, while the independent house offers another scale of occupation for focused support and small-group learning. Their relationship is that of neighboring institutions on shared grounds, not an enclosed three-part circulation network. The scheme seeks to provide a distinct setting for intensive support while retaining direct academic access to communal activities and allowing the separate house to establish its own daily rhythm.

Three independent school houses face a common outdoor forum, making the open ground the organizing centre rather than an enclosed corridor. A taller teaching house establishes one edge, a separate support and cultural house forms another, and the communal hall completes the constellation. Each building keeps its own threshold, so relationships occur through the shared exterior rather than constructed links. The teaching house rises three storeys with classrooms throughout. The support house rises two, with administration and arts at grade and reading above; the independent commons remains a low double-height volume. Core academic occupies its own teaching house; special education and administration share a separate support house. Gym and dining form the third independent destination, with all three related through outdoor space.

Three independent school houses face a common outdoor forum, making the open ground the organizing centre rather than an enclosed corridor. A taller teaching house establishes one edge, a separate support and cultural house forms another, and the communal hall completes the constellation. Each building keeps its own threshold, so relationships occur through the shared exterior rather than constructed links. The scheme seeks to encourage outdoor encounters among different school communities while maintaining independent identities and operational boundaries for teaching, support and collective events.

Two parallel inhabited ranges establish separate but complementary school streets. One is a continuous teaching environment; the other combines arrival, cultural activity and community gathering into a layered public range. A smaller support house connects the two at one end, creating a sheltered circulation circuit without enclosing a courtyard. The assembly volume anchors the public range rather than occupying an independent central block. The teaching range rises three floors with classrooms above its ground level. The public range stays double height around gathering spaces. The support house rises three floors, with administration at grade and reading at its crown. Core academic occupies the taller teaching range, while special education shares its quieter teaching environment. Administration occupies the connecting support house, mediating access to the parallel commons range containing gym and dining.

Two parallel inhabited ranges establish separate but complementary school streets. One is a continuous teaching environment; the other combines arrival, cultural activity and community gathering into a layered public range. A smaller support house connects the two at one end, creating a sheltered circulation circuit without enclosing a courtyard. The assembly volume anchors the public range rather than occupying an independent central block. Seeks to distinguish everyday teaching circulation from community activity while retaining an enclosed route between them, with a support house providing a controlled transition for students and visitors.

Two teaching-related houses form a paired educational precinct, while the commons stands apart as a separate community destination. The principal classroom house establishes the daily academic center. A neighboring inclusion and civic house accommodates more individualized learning and public-facing support. The freestanding hall belongs to the same school grounds but is not part of an enclosed circulation loop or courtyard perimeter. Both educational houses rise three floors, with general classrooms occupying the taller academic sequence and administration at the base of the companion house below a reading crown. The freestanding commons remains double height. Core academic occupies one educational house, directly linked to a second house containing special education and administration. Gym and dining occupy a separate commons building reached outdoors rather than through either educational house.

Two teaching-related houses form a paired educational precinct, while the commons stands apart as a separate community destination. The principal classroom house establishes the daily academic center. A neighboring inclusion and civic house accommodates more individualized learning and public-facing support. The freestanding hall belongs to the same school grounds but is not part of an enclosed circulation loop or courtyard perimeter. Seeks to establish distinguishable learning environments for general and individualized teaching, while allowing the community commons to operate as a separate destination without occupying the center of school circulation.

A communal crossing separates two complementary educational territories: a general learning house and a specialized learning house. The gym and dining volume occupies the crossing, becoming the only enclosed route between the two. Both educational houses rise above a lower communal middle, giving the school a paired identity rather than one dominant academic center. The specialized house also establishes the school's civic face. Both educational houses rise three storeys. The general house carries classrooms throughout; the specialized house begins with administration and arts, supports inclusive teaching above and ends in reading. The central commons remains double-height and low. Core academic and special education occupy separate teaching houses across the commons. Administration shares the specialized house at ground level, while the gym and dining form the common territory connecting both educational communities.

A communal crossing separates two complementary educational territories: a general learning house and a specialized learning house. The gym and dining volume occupies the crossing, becoming the only enclosed route between the two. Both educational houses rise above a lower communal middle, giving the school a paired identity rather than one dominant academic center. The specialized house also establishes the school's civic face. The scheme seeks to make shared activity an intentional meeting point between general and specialized education while allowing each teaching territory to retain a distinct internal organization and atmosphere.

A layered school is organized around a controlled civic filter separating a concentrated teaching house from a tall shared-activity house. The middle building is conceived as a sequence of thresholds rather than simply a connector: it mediates between protected daily learning and collective events. Above the gathering volumes, specialist teaching forms a distinct upper setting within the communal house. All three masses rise to three storeys. The academic house layers classrooms above ground-level arts; the civic filter rises from administration and care to a reading crown. The commons places double-height gathering below upper-level special education. Core academic occupies one end of the chain, while special education shares the opposite commons house with gym and dining. Administration occupies the intervening civic filter, the sole enclosed route between them.

A layered school is organized around a controlled civic filter separating a concentrated teaching house from a tall shared-activity house. The middle building is conceived as a sequence of thresholds rather than simply a connector: it mediates between protected daily learning and collective events. Above the gathering volumes, specialist teaching forms a distinct upper setting within the communal house. The scheme seeks to maintain a clear administrative threshold between teaching and community activity while placing specialist support within reach of communal learning and shared facilities.

The school revolves around an inclusive commons conceived as a shared threshold rather than a conventional assembly hall. Everyday teaching approaches it from one side, and the school's civic and cultural activities approach from the other. Specialist support is embedded in this collective middle ground, allowing the commons to act as a carefully managed meeting place between academic and community routines. All three masses remain low at two storeys. Classrooms occupy both academic levels; the civic house places arts and administration at grade with reading above. The central commons rises through two levels as a double-height gathering volume. Core academic occupies one wing, connecting only to the commons. Special education shares that central mass with gym and dining at ground level; administration occupies the opposite wing, reached through the commons.

The school revolves around an inclusive commons conceived as a shared threshold rather than a conventional assembly hall. Everyday teaching approaches it from one side, and the school's civic and cultural activities approach from the other. Specialist support is embedded in this collective middle ground, allowing the commons to act as a carefully managed meeting place between academic and community routines. The scheme seeks to make supported participation in collective school life central to the educational experience while retaining distinct academic and civic domains on either side of the shared threshold.

A three-storey cultural threshold separates two different institutional worlds: a concentrated academy and a communal house that combines gathering with specialized care. The threshold is the only built passage between them, conceived as a sequence of creative and reading environments rather than a conventional administrative crossroads. Its layered activities give the intermediate building an inhabited identity of its own. All masses reach three storeys. Teaching occupies the academy vertically; the middle house places administration and arts at grade with reading at its crown; the commons holds double-height gathering below upper specialized support. Core academic occupies one end, while special education shares the opposite commons mass with gym and dining. Ground-floor administration and the cultural program occupy the intermediate mass, which alone connects those destinations.

A three-storey cultural threshold separates two different institutional worlds: a concentrated academy and a communal house that combines gathering with specialized care. The threshold is the only built passage between them, conceived as a sequence of creative and reading environments rather than a conventional administrative crossroads. Its layered activities give the intermediate building an inhabited identity of its own. The scheme seeks to buffer general classrooms from large communal events while making cultural activities a shared destination and keeping specialized support close to collective school life.

The school separates into a quieter learning island and a connected public dock. The learning island contains the everyday educational community, including specialized instruction, but remains physically independent. The public dock is a paired composition: a large gathering hall directly attached to a taller cultural and administrative house. Shared grounds connect these two realms without an enclosed route between school teaching and civic activities. The detached learning house rises three storeys, combining classrooms with lower-level specialized learning and care. The public hall stays double-height and low, while its attached civic house rises to an upper reading floor. Core academic and special education share the independent learning house. Administration sits at ground level in the civic house, directly connected to gym and dining, creating a public-facing pair separate from teaching.

The school separates into a quieter learning island and a connected public dock. The learning island contains the everyday educational community, including specialized instruction, but remains physically independent. The public dock is a paired composition: a large gathering hall directly attached to a taller cultural and administrative house. Shared grounds connect these two realms without an enclosed route between school teaching and civic activities. The scheme seeks to establish a strong communal destination for cultural events and school gathering while protecting the teaching environment from the circulation and activity associated with larger public functions.

Three equally developed building parts form an interconnected school with several ways to move between daily teaching, shared cultural life and assembly. Rather than organizing circulation around one obligatory crossroads or courtyard, the scheme uses direct links between every pair to create alternative internal routes. Each part maintains its own identity while participating in a continuous network of school life. Each mass reaches three storeys. Learning and special education rise together; the commons places gathering volumes at grade with an arts loft above. The civic house begins with administration and care, carries service space and ends in reading. Core academic and special education share the vertical teaching house. Administration sits in an adjoining civic house, while gym and dining occupy the third, communal mass; both have direct connections to learning and each other.

Three equally developed building parts form an interconnected school with several ways to move between daily teaching, shared cultural life and assembly. Rather than organizing circulation around one obligatory crossroads or courtyard, the scheme uses direct links between every pair to create alternative internal routes. Each part maintains its own identity while participating in a continuous network of school life. The scheme seeks to distribute movement across multiple connections, give staff alternative routes between activities and reduce dependence on a single communal passage during daily transitions.

A teaching house, a specialist cultural house and a collective activity house form a three-part academic neighborhood. None is subordinated to a dominant school bar or a small workshop hinge. All three connect directly, allowing daily school life to circulate among complementary destinations while keeping large assembly activities outside the main teaching house. The teaching and specialist houses rise three floors. Classrooms fill the teaching house; special education and arts occupy the specialist house below its upper reading spaces. The commons remains a low double-height destination with support at grade. Core academic forms one teaching house, while special education sits alongside administration in a directly connected specialist house. Gym and dining share the third mass, linked directly to both learning environments.

A teaching house, a specialist cultural house and a collective activity house form a three-part academic neighborhood. None is subordinated to a dominant school bar or a small workshop hinge. All three connect directly, allowing daily school life to circulate among complementary destinations while keeping large assembly activities outside the main teaching house. The scheme seeks to create a balanced set of learning destinations, giving specialized teaching an identifiable place without separating it from general classrooms, administrative care or collective school activities.

Three connected houses form a circulation triangle organized around route choice rather than a courtyard or shared central room. The learning house and the civic-arts house each connect directly to the commons, while a third enclosed connection joins them independently. The resulting network offers a pupil route, a public route and a cross-school route without assigning any single house the role of compulsory passage. The learning house rises three floors to an upper media center alongside classrooms. The civic-arts house remains lower, with administration and arts at grade and arts continuing above. The commons stays double height. Core academic and special education share the learning house, while administration occupies a separate but directly connected civic-arts house. Both have independent enclosed connections to the gym and dining commons.

Three connected houses form a circulation triangle organized around route choice rather than a courtyard or shared central room. The learning house and the civic-arts house each connect directly to the commons, while a third enclosed connection joins them independently. The resulting network offers a pupil route, a public route and a cross-school route without assigning any single house the role of compulsory passage. The scheme seeks to separate everyday pupil circulation from visitor movement while retaining direct connections between teaching, administration and communal activities.

A consolidated learning core is paired with two different activity satellites: one dedicated to making and student care, the other to large collective gatherings. The satellites connect independently to the core but not to each other. Rather than organizing movement through a hall or civic hinge, the academic core becomes the sole enclosed interchange between specialized activity environments. The academic core rises three floors, with administration at grade, classrooms distributed vertically and reading at the top. The making satellite remains low, while the commons forms a separate double-height volume. Core academic, special education and administration share the central learning block. Gym and dining occupy one satellite, while arts and care occupy the other, keeping both activity environments adjacent to teaching.

A consolidated learning core is paired with two different activity satellites: one dedicated to making and student care, the other to large collective gatherings. The satellites connect independently to the core but not to each other. Rather than organizing movement through a hall or civic hinge, the academic core becomes the sole enclosed interchange between specialized activity environments. The scheme seeks to protect an identifiable academic center while allowing creative support and large-group activity to operate as distinct destinations with separate operational identities.

A reading bridge establishes the school's principal shared connection above ground, joining a classroom tower to a cultural house. Below it, the classroom and cultural realms remain distinct, while a separate commons building connects directly to the cultural house. The resulting arrangement makes the elevated library the academic crossing and the cultural house the transition toward assembly. The classroom tower rises three floors, and the cultural house rises to an upper media center that forms the elevated link. The commons remains double-height, with gym and dining at grade. Core academic learning occupies the tower, while special education and administration share the cultural house. Gym and dining occupy a separate connected commons, making the cultural house the transition between teaching and assembly.

A reading bridge establishes the school's principal shared connection above ground, joining a classroom tower to a cultural house. Below it, the classroom and cultural realms remain distinct, while a separate commons building connects directly to the cultural house. The resulting arrangement makes the elevated library the academic crossing and the cultural house the transition toward assembly. The scheme seeks to make reading a visible shared destination while distinguishing the quieter academic environment from communal assembly and allowing cultural activities to mediate between them.

The school unfolds as a sequence of increasingly collective territories. A tall learning house leads into a lower civic gallery, which acts as a shared threshold before reaching an assembly house. Rather than separating inclusive support from communal activity, the assembly house develops an upper care terrace above its gathering volumes. The gallery remains the only built connection between the two taller houses. The learning house rises three storeys, with classrooms throughout. The gallery stays two storeys, placing administration and arts at grade and reading above. The assembly house rises three storeys, lifting specialized learning over double-height communal volumes. Core academic teaching occupies one end of the sequence, while special education shares the opposite assembly house with gym and dining. Ground-floor administration occupies the intermediate gallery, controlling passage between the two.

The school unfolds as a sequence of increasingly collective territories. A tall learning house leads into a lower civic gallery, which acts as a shared threshold before reaching an assembly house. Rather than separating inclusive support from communal activity, the assembly house develops an upper care terrace above its gathering volumes. The gallery remains the only built connection between the two taller houses. The strategy seeks to give specialized learners a recognizable place within communal school life while using the intermediate civic gallery to mediate movement, supervision and transitions between teaching and assembly.

The learning house becomes the spatial hinge rather than the civic front or the assembly hall. A taller teaching spine connects directly to two distinct destinations: a quieter civic and support house and a broad community commons. Those destinations remain disconnected from each other, making the learning spine the only enclosed route between them. The learning spine rises three floors, with art at grade and classrooms continuing to the top. The civic house rises to a library crown above administration and specialist teaching. The commons stays low and double height. Core academic occupies the connecting spine, while special education and administration share the quieter destination. Gym and dining occupy the opposite destination, reached directly from the learning spine rather than through the civic house.

The learning house becomes the spatial hinge rather than the civic front or the assembly hall. A taller teaching spine connects directly to two distinct destinations: a quieter civic and support house and a broad community commons. Those destinations remain disconnected from each other, making the learning spine the only enclosed route between them. The scheme seeks to make everyday teaching space the organizing reference for students while allowing civic support and shared activities to remain distinct destinations.

A linear school sequence is organized around an inclusive teaching threshold rather than a civic gateway or workshop pavilion. The principal academic house connects to a smaller specialist house that serves as a transition toward communal activities. Beyond that threshold stands the hall. Special education, creative learning and care occupy the intermediate realm, making it an educational destination as well as the passage to the commons. The principal academic house rises three floors, with administration at grade and the media center crowning classrooms. The intermediate house rises two floors around specialist teaching, with arts and care at grade. The commons remains double height. Core academic and administration share the principal house. Special education occupies the intermediate house alongside arts and medical support, separating general classrooms from gym and dining while providing their only enclosed connection.

A linear school sequence is organized around an inclusive teaching threshold rather than a civic gateway or workshop pavilion. The principal academic house connects to a smaller specialist house that serves as a transition toward communal activities. Beyond that threshold stands the hall. Special education, creative learning and care occupy the intermediate realm, making it an educational destination as well as the passage to the commons. The scheme seeks to make specialized learning and creative activity visible within everyday school movement while retaining a clear progression from general teaching toward communal activities.

A vertical academy anchors one end of the school, while a compact care-oriented threshold mediates its relationship with the community hall. Unlike a conventional gateway devoted primarily to public arrival, this middle house is an inhabited support environment. Its specialist spaces establish a transition from the concentrated teaching tower to the collective activities beyond. The academy rises three floors, with classrooms above its ground-level teaching base and reading at its crown. The care threshold reaches three floors from administration and medical support to arts above. The double-height hall stays low. Core academic occupies the academy, directly connected to administration and special education in the care threshold. The commons lies beyond that threshold, separating collective activity from the academic tower without isolating specialist support.

A vertical academy anchors one end of the school, while a compact care-oriented threshold mediates its relationship with the community hall. Unlike a conventional gateway devoted primarily to public arrival, this middle house is an inhabited support environment. Its specialist spaces establish a transition from the concentrated teaching tower to the collective activities beyond. The scheme seeks to give the school a recognizable vertical academic identity while making inclusive support part of everyday transitions between classrooms, school services and communal activities.

The school is organized as three independent neighborhood houses rather than one enclosed institution. A tall general learning house establishes the everyday classroom identity; a separate care and civic house serves as a specialized educational destination; a low assembly pavilion accommodates collective events. Each house stands on shared grounds without a built link, treating outdoor movement as the relationship between distinct educational settings. The classroom house and care-civic house each rise three storeys, with classrooms or administration at grade and learning or reading above. The independent assembly pavilion remains a lower double-height volume. Core academic classrooms occupy an independent tall house, while special education and administration share a second house with supporting care and culture. Gym and dining remain together in a separate low pavilion.

The school is organized as three independent neighborhood houses rather than one enclosed institution. A tall general learning house establishes the everyday classroom identity; a separate care and civic house serves as a specialized educational destination; a low assembly pavilion accommodates collective events. Each house stands on shared grounds without a built link, treating outdoor movement as the relationship between distinct educational settings. This strategy seeks to make specialized education a recognizable, self-contained school community while giving ordinary teaching and larger gatherings independent identities and potentially different operating patterns.

The school is organized as a teaching house with a community porch attached to its side, rather than as a sequence of buildings connected by a civic gateway. A compact arrival and care house sits beside the teaching house and shares its internal circulation. The commons connects directly to the teaching house but remains separate from the arrival house, giving the campus two distinct internal thresholds. The teaching house and arrival house rise three floors. Classrooms extend upward in the teaching house, while administration anchors the arrival house below its reading crown. The attached commons remains double height at grade. Core academic and special education share a vertically organized teaching house. Ground-floor administration sits in the adjacent arrival house, while gym and dining attach to teaching circulation rather than forming the endpoint of a civic gateway.

The school is organized as a teaching house with a community porch attached to its side, rather than as a sequence of buildings connected by a civic gateway. A compact arrival and care house sits beside the teaching house and shares its internal circulation. The commons connects directly to the teaching house but remains separate from the arrival house, giving the campus two distinct internal thresholds. Seeks to provide a recognizable civic threshold while preventing all classroom-to-commons movement from passing through reception, enabling school-day circulation and supervised community access to operate differently.

A low campus sequence treats the shared commons as an inhabited passage between a compact civic house and a quieter learning retreat. The communal building becomes the crossing point between two contrasting environments, with supervised support attached to the rhythm of gathering and dining. The three parts connect in sequence, and their lower profiles emphasize a horizontal progression rather than a vertically stacked institution. All masses stay at two storeys. The learning retreat distributes classrooms across both levels; the commons places double-height gathering at grade beneath upper specialized teaching; the civic house carries ground-floor administration and arts below reading. Core academic occupies the quiet learning end, while special education occupies the commons with gym and dining. Administration occupies the civic end, connected to the learning mass only through the commons.

A low campus sequence treats the shared commons as an inhabited passage between a compact civic house and a quieter learning retreat. The communal building becomes the crossing point between two contrasting environments, with supervised support attached to the rhythm of gathering and dining. The three parts connect in sequence, and their lower profiles emphasize a horizontal progression rather than a vertically stacked institution. The proposal seeks to link student support with everyday communal routines while giving general classrooms a quieter destination beyond shared activity and maintaining a distinct civic front.

A self-contained school spine holds daily teaching, care, administration and reading within one connected vertical institution. Beyond it, two detached communal satellites form a complementary public realm: a double-height assembly building and a separate cultural workshop house. The cultural house gathers creative learning and building operations, allowing shared activity to develop outside the academic spine without occupying a loft over the hall. The main school spine rises three floors, from administration and care at grade through teaching to reading above. The workshop satellite occupies a low level, while the separate commons forms a double-height ground-floor volume. Core academic and special education share the main spine with ground-floor administration. Gym and dining form one freestanding satellite, while arts occupy another, separating community and creative activity from the main academic circulation.

A self-contained school spine holds daily teaching, care, administration and reading within one connected vertical institution. Beyond it, two detached communal satellites form a complementary public realm: a double-height assembly building and a separate cultural workshop house. The cultural house gathers creative learning and building operations, allowing shared activity to develop outside the academic spine without occupying a loft over the hall. Seeks to keep essential daily educational functions in one school building while presenting creative activity and community assembly as distinct destinations that can support activities beyond regular classroom use.

Three distinct masses form a pair of parallel institutional streets rather than a centralized hub or sequential chain. A classroom house and a shared activity house establish separate daily territories, while a narrower cultural house connects them at two points. The connections create alternative internal routes without making any single mass an obligatory crossroads. The classroom house rises three floors, with teaching distributed upward. The cultural house also reaches three floors, placing administration at grade, arts on the middle level and reading at the top. The double-height commons remains low. Core academic and special education share the tall classroom house, while administration occupies the adjoining cultural house. Gym and dining stay together in the parallel activity house, accessible without crossing the classrooms.

Three distinct masses form a pair of parallel institutional streets rather than a centralized hub or sequential chain. A classroom house and a shared activity house establish separate daily territories, while a narrower cultural house connects them at two points. The connections create alternative internal routes without making any single mass an obligatory crossroads. The scheme seeks to separate concentrated learning from collective activity while allowing students and staff to circulate through different routes and encounter shared cultural spaces without compulsory passage through assembly areas.

Two vertically developed buildings form the school's primary connected pair: a teaching academy and a communal forum. A third building operates as a separate care and cultural house, occupying the same campus but remaining outside the enclosed circulation network. The academy-to-forum connection establishes the principal institutional relationship, while the detached house creates a parallel destination rather than another intermediate gateway. All three masses reach three storeys. The academy rises through teaching levels, the forum places double-height gym and dining at grade beneath a third-floor arts level, and the separate house places administration below specialist support and top-floor reading. Core academic occupies the academy connected directly to gym and dining. Special education occupies a detached third mass with ground-floor administration; the commons therefore connects to general classrooms without passing through specialized support.

Two vertically developed buildings form the school's primary connected pair: a teaching academy and a communal forum. A third building operates as a separate care and cultural house, occupying the same campus but remaining outside the enclosed circulation network. The academy-to-forum connection establishes the principal institutional relationship, while the detached house creates a parallel destination rather than another intermediate gateway. The strategy seeks to establish a strong relationship between teaching and gathering while giving specialized student support a more independent setting and separating its circulation from large communal events.

A school street unfolds as a sequence of three distinct places: an academic house, an inhabited care passage, and a collective activity hall. The middle place is conceived as a quieter social threshold rather than a conventional civic foyer. Its connection to the hall allows support spaces to participate in communal life while the learning house retains a separate identity. The academic house rises three storeys, with classrooms from grade to roof. The middle care passage rises two storeys, with arts at grade and reading above; the low commons retains double-height volumes. Core academic occupies the tall end house, while special education shares the middle passage with administration and support. Gym and dining occupy the opposite end, directly adjoining special education rather than classrooms.

A school street unfolds as a sequence of three distinct places: an academic house, an inhabited care passage, and a collective activity hall. The middle place is conceived as a quieter social threshold rather than a conventional civic foyer. Its connection to the hall allows support spaces to participate in communal life while the learning house retains a separate identity. The scheme seeks to make specialized support part of everyday school life while establishing a recognizable transition between concentrated learning and noisy collective activities.

A continuous learning spine becomes the inhabited connector between two otherwise separate pavilions. One pavilion presents a civic and cultural face, while the other contains the larger shared activities. The spine is not merely a corridor: teaching neighborhoods occupy its length, and its opposite ends establish distinct transitions to the two pavilions. The arrangement remains predominantly low and horizontally organized. All three masses remain at two storeys. Classrooms and specialist teaching occupy both learning levels; administration and arts remain at grade in the civic pavilion, with reading above. The commons remains double height. Core academic and special education share the central learning spine. Administration occupies one connected end, while gym and dining occupy the other, making the learning mass the sole built connection between them.

A continuous learning spine becomes the inhabited connector between two otherwise separate pavilions. One pavilion presents a civic and cultural face, while the other contains the larger shared activities. The spine is not merely a corridor: teaching neighborhoods occupy its length, and its opposite ends establish distinct transitions to the two pavilions. The arrangement remains predominantly low and horizontally organized. The scheme seeks to make daily teaching the organizing center of school circulation while allowing civic activities and larger communal gatherings to retain distinct identities and operating boundaries.

The school is conceived as a compact, low educational cloister formed by a learning house and an attached civic porch. The learning house combines ordinary and specialized classrooms into one teaching community; the porch provides a contrasting setting for making, reading and school administration. A separate gathering pavilion sits beyond this paired institution, connected through shared outdoor school life rather than an enclosed passage. All three masses remain low. Classrooms and specialized learning occupy two teaching levels. The connected civic porch places administration and arts at grade with reading above. The detached commons is double-height.
